title: AI in Finance, Lesson 10: Writing a financial memo with AI
subtitle: From scattered data to a memo that is short, clear and carries its risks.
openingQuestion: What does a good financial memo need?
openingOptions: A conclusion, evidence, risks and what still needs checking
explanation: A financial memo is a short document letting the reader grasp the conclusion, the evidence and the risks in a few minutes. It is the practical output of a great deal of analytical work, and it is where AI helps most: it produces a structured draft very fast. But an AI draft has an inherent weakness - it writes fluently even where the evidence is thin, so a confident sentence can hide an argument with no figures behind it. Your job is to examine each claim and cut whatever cannot be proved.

summary.keyIdea: AI writes the draft, but you must check the figures and the risks before sending it.
summary.commonMistake: Sending the AI's draft as written, without checking sources or tone.
summary.action: Ask AI to write a one-page memo from an article or a set of accounts, then verify 3 figures yourself.

sections.text: A memo is a short note letting the reader make a decision, or know what to check next.

sections.label: Terms
sections.text: Memo: a short note. One-pager: a single-page document. Investment thesis: the central argument for why to invest or not.
From the information below, write a one-page memo. Include: conclusion, evidence, risks, missing data, questions to verify. Do not invent figures.
Check the sources of the figures, the units, the risks and the tone. What goes out is your responsibility, not the AI's.

sections.title: The five-part frame and what counts as done

concepts.def: At most 2-3 sentences, stating plainly what you believe and how confident you are. If the reader has 2 minutes, this part has to be enough.
Three main claims, each with figures and a source. Without a number it is an opinion rather than evidence.
The two largest risks, specific enough that the reader knows what to watch. Avoid generic risks such as "market volatility".
The information you needed and do not have. This part makes the memo more credible rather than weaker.
Specific actions: which note to look up, whom to ask, which metric to watch next quarter.

sections.label: A full prompt to reuse
sections.text: "Using only the data I provide below, write a memo of at most 500 words in exactly 5 sections: Conclusion (2-3 sentences), Evidence (3 claims, each one required to carry figures and a source), Risks (2 specific risks), Missing data, Next steps. Do not use evaluative adjectives without figures alongside. Do not give a buy or sell recommendation. Where a section lacks data, say so rather than writing generically."

items: Pass 1 - the figures: reopen the source, reconcile each number, check the units and the reporting period.
Pass 2 - the claims: underline every evaluative adjective, ask "which number proves this?", and cut whatever cannot answer.
Pass 3 - the reader: give it to someone who knows nothing about the business, let them read for 2 minutes, and ask them to restate the conclusion and the risks.

sections.text: If the reader in pass 3 restates it wrongly, the problem is the memo rather than the reader. A good memo is not the best written one but the one hardest to misread.

lines: AI drafts fast; you make it trustworthy.
A good memo is one that leaves the reader knowing what to ask next.

quiz.question: What does memo mean?
options: A share price table
An audit report
A short written note
A loan agreement
quiz.explanation: Memo is the term commonly used for a short written note.

quiz.question: What must you do before sending an AI-written draft?
options: Ask the AI whether the draft is rigorous enough
Polish the prose so it reads more smoothly still
Add a chart to illustrate the conclusion section
Check the sources, figures, units and risks
quiz.explanation: AI drafts; whoever sends it is responsible for the quality.

quiz.question: Why does a "missing data" section make a memo more credible?
options: Because it tells the reader the boundary of the conclusion
Because it proves you read every source document
Because it makes the memo longer and more complete
Because it is a mandatory section under reporting standards
quiz.explanation: A conclusion stating what it rests on and what it does not know is checkable. A conclusion that looks completely certain has usually hidden the unknown part.

quiz.question: What is the fastest way to spot an unsupported claim in an AI draft?
options: Read the draft backwards from the final paragraph to the first
Underline every evaluative adjective and ask which figure supports it
Count how many times the draft mentions the company's name
Ask a different AI to rewrite it and compare the two versions
quiz.explanation: Evaluative adjectives - "positive", "leading", "improving", "sustainable" - are exactly where judgment slips in among the facts. Keep them where a number exists; cut them where none does.

quiz.question: What is the quick way to check a memo written by AI?
options: Compare its length against the memos written in previous periods
Read it start to finish to check the coherence of the whole argument
Read backwards from the conclusion, asking what evidence each sentence rests on
Ask the AI to rate the reliability of each section it has just written
quiz.explanation: Reading forwards lets fluent prose carry you along. Reading backwards forces every assertion to stand on its own evidence, and the sentences with nothing underneath them show up immediately.

realWorldExample.company: A confident sentence hiding a weak claim
realWorldExample.description: One sentence pattern appears constantly in AI drafts: "With its leading industry position and improving margins, the business has a positive growth outlook over the medium term." It reads smoothly and contains three unsupported assertions: leading on what criterion and from what data, margins improving from what level to what level, and how long "medium term" is. A simple test: underline every evaluative adjective in the draft, and for each one ask "which figure proves this?". Any sentence that cannot answer either gets a number added or gets deleted.

keyTakeaways: The five-part frame: conclusion, evidence, risks, missing data, next steps.
The "missing data" section is what earns credibility - do not drop it to make the memo look more certain.
Underline every evaluative adjective and demand a figure; where there is none, cut it.
Reconcile the draft's figures against the source before sending - the responsibility is yours.

practicePrompt.question: What does a good financial memo need?
options: A conclusion, evidence, risks and what still needs checking
Praise only
Attractive icons only
No figures at all
practicePrompt.explanation: A good memo has to let the reader grasp the conclusion and what it rests on.

application.title: Try it now
application.message: Ask AI to write a one-page memo from an article or a set of accounts, then verify 3 figures yourself.
application.secondary: Start small, verify clearly, and only then raise the difficulty.

whyItMatters: A memo is what other people read and decide on - your name is on it, not the AI's.
